source.title: When is early stopping beneficial under label noise? A phase diagram for kernel gradient flow

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper, including appendices; no material cutoff noted.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly tracks test error and classification of randomly labeled examples during training, using partial label corruption and kernel dynamics rather than the original full-random-label experiment.
record.gate_note: The neural-network experiments report classification error on a randomized subset, not training error on a completely randomly labeled training set. The reported positive MSE also means zero classification error should not be read as exact interpolation. The cited Zhang et al. and Arpit et al. findings are prior work, not this study's results. Figure-only numerical values are not transcribed.
record.test_reason: The neural-network experiments directly measure fitting of randomly labeled subsets and clean-task generalization in new architectures and training recipes. They bear on V4's coexistence of signal learning and noise memorization and V5's data-augmentation component. They do not reproduce the fully random-label experiment.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's empirical paraphrase is accurate but incomplete. The authors also derive a kernel-geometry boundary separating finite-time optimal stopping from convergence-optimal learning, and identify a critical kernel whose interpolating endpoint achieves the lowest test error across the considered kernel family and training times. They do not establish that trained deep networks acquire this geometry.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies partial label corruption and early-stopping effects in CIFAR10 networks and kernel gradient flow; it does not reproduce the original all-random-label experiment. Neural-network recipes include square-loss SGD and augmented cross-entropy with scheduled learning rates.
record.method_sensitivity: The size of late test-error deterioration varies with architecture and capacity, kernel bandwidth, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, training-set size, random-label fraction, and whether randomized examples are automobiles or cats and dogs. For kernel gradient flow, the stopping regime varies with kernel geometry.

fits_no_version.finding: Fixed-feature and shallow models deteriorate late in training, whereas larger deep models have little observed early-stopping benefit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The generalization cost of completing noise memorization depends on architecture and capacity.

fits_no_version.finding: Kernel geometry determines early-stopping benefit, and a critical kernel interpolates while minimizing test error across the considered kernels and times.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the stated synthetic-data assumptions, kernel geometry can make interpolation optimal despite irreducible label noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Synthetic RBF experiments exhibit either delayed rule generalization after factual memorization or useful generalization before factual memorization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The ordering of rule generalization and random-label memorization in kernel dynamics depends on initialization and kernel geometry.

record.problems: Neural-network results use partial label corruption, and the randomized-label measure is classification error rather than exact training loss. The square-loss training MSE remains positive at the reported horizon. Several detailed comparisons are presented in figures; the paper notes finite gaps and small numerical fluctuations. The model experiments do not establish behavior on a completely random labeling of the full training set.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. The paper has many figure-based sweeps and parameter combinations; their exact per-condition values are not recoverable from the supplied prose without reading precise plot values. The selected rows preserve the textual outcomes and named conditions relevant to V4 and V5.

untested.parts: Completely random labels on the entire training set, chance test error in that condition, and fitting without changing the true-label architecture or hyperparameters.
True-label versus random-label training-time ratios and a quantified convergence slowdown as corruption increases.
Deep-network fitting of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs. Synthetic spherical inputs trained with a kernel do not test this version.

Perfect classification of the entire training set; the fully randomized endpoint; a demonstrated steady test-error rise toward chance across corruption fractions. Most rows use only a fixed 20% randomized subset.

Fitting fully random labels despite weight decay or dropout; separate effects of the named regularizers; a controlled demonstration that removing explicit regularization preserves good generalization on wholly true-labeled data.

A direct deep-network comparison establishing that shared real-label patterns are learned before noisy labels. Best test performance occurring after noise classification is complete does not establish or refute that ordering.

record.verdict_notes: Late test-error deterioration over training is distinct from V4's test-error trend across noise fractions. Neither shallow-model deterioration nor untested monotonicity warrants the record's limits_scope labels. Positive MSE does not rule out zero classification error, but randomized-subset accuracy alone does not establish whole-training-set accuracy.

versions.untested_parts: The study randomizes only a fraction of the training labels; it does not test completely random labels on the entire training set, chance test error under that condition, or the full conjunction in the version.
No comparison of training time for true versus random labels or convergence slowdown as corruption rises.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

The study varies random-label fraction and measures test error and randomized-subset classification error, but does not establish a steady monotonic rise of test error toward chance or that networks capture all remaining signal. Its primary CIFAR10 experiments use a 20% randomized subset.

Tests augmented training with no weight decay, dropout, or label smoothing, and separately reports no-augmentation/no-weight-decay protocols. It does not isolate each regularizer or establish that removing regularization by itself causes poor true-label generalization.
The paper cites prior work on learning shared structure before memorization, but does not test whether real and random labels are learned differently over training.

rows.operation_detail: Full-batch readout gradient descent on square loss; fixed randomized automobiles and clean cat-dog labels; no augmentation or weight decay.

conditions.value: CIFAR10; 2800 cats, 2800 dogs, 1400 automobiles with independent random labels

rows.measure: Clean cat-dog test error versus classification error on randomized automobiles
rows.value: Fixed-feature and smaller or shallower models exhibit late-time test-error deterioration as memorization error decreases.
rows.uncertainty: Curves average about 30 completed seeds; exact uncertainty not stated for this comparison.
rows.note: Text groups fixed-feature and shallower models qualitatively; no per-model numerical values are stated in prose.
rows.check: Only an affine readout is trained over frozen random features. This is not evidence about training standard deep networks as named in the versions. The reported deterioration concerns early stopping.

rows.measure: Test error and classification error on randomized training examples

rows.uncertainty: Five seeds, with ten seeds at ε = 0.1 and 0.2 for Figure 12; bars show one sample standard deviation.

Missing evidence of that trend is not an observed scope limitation. Square-loss horizons are 200 epochs for n=9216, 300 for ε=0.6, and 400 otherwise.
